newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya Airways profit falls 39.5 percent.
newsitem.headline: Kenya Airways profit falls 39.5 percent.

text.p: National carrier Kenya Airways full year profits went down 39.5 percent despite a marginal rise in turnover, airline officials said on Tuesday.
A statement issued by the airline said the decline was expected following an increase in fuel and labour costs but was aggravated by a strong shilling in the period.

"The bulk of our earnings are in foreign currencies. They're greatly influenced by the behaviour of the Kenyan shilling and for that period the shilling was strong," Koome Mwambia, the airlines spokesman told Reuters.
Net profit after tax for the year ended 31 March 1997 was posted at 851.6 million shillings ($14.4 million) compared to 1.419 billion shillings for the previous year.
Officials said the shilling's continued strength against the dollar generated a loss of 322 million shillings compared to a profit of 400.2 million shillings in the previous year.
However, brokers said they were not too alarmed.
"They were not unexpected (referring to a difficult operating year). The issue of forex is a factor beyond their control," a senior broker said.
"The results just highlight the vulnerability of exporters to foreign exchange risk. In fact we will expect similar results from exporters," a market analyst said.
A 200 percent increase in pay and benefits to the airline's pilots was the biggest reason for a 27 percent rise in labour costs.
Total costs this year went up to 9.3 billion shillings from 8.449 billion shillings from last year -- a 10.1 percent increase.
"In fact the long-term prospects look good," another broker said.
They said the company was poised for a better year on increased capacity and the possibility of a weaker shilling in the remaining half of the year.
"A depreciation to 58 shillings against the dollar from the levels of 53/54 which was used to calculate their earnings should be enough to eliminate the forex loss," one analyst said.
Mwambia said the airline acquisition of two new Boeing 737-300 aircraft between March and May would help stimulate demand. He added the airline was set to acquire another in May 1998.
For speculators, the announcement would do nothing to bolster their confidence in the share, brokers said.
Disappointed by the shares downturn last year to levels as low as seven shillings from the initial offer price of 11.25, when it went public, they flooded the market with shares.
"They offloaded their shares into the market and drove the price down," one analyst said.
